title: Rate limits are a continuously refilling allowance that repaying debt restores, not a cumulative cap
content:
A.6.1.1.5.2.6.1.2.2.1.3.4 gives the exact formula: the contract "will calculate and return the minimum of (slope * time elapsed since lastUpdated + lastAmount) and maxAmount." Consuming capacity is the mirror image — `triggerRateLimitDecrease` sets "lastAmount to currentRateLimit minus amountToDecrease" and stamps the current timestamp (A.6.1.1.5.2.6.1.2.2.1.3.5).

This is a token bucket: `maxAmount` is the bucket size, `slope` the refill rate per second, and every operation drains it by its size. Nothing is ever counted cumulatively, so a Liquidity Layer running for years faces the same constraint as one running for a week — the limit governs *velocity*, not lifetime volume.

The reflexive case is where it becomes a risk instrument rather than a throttle. `burnUSDS` "will increase the available Rate Limit for minting USDS by the amount of USDS being burned. This increase will be limited by the `maxAmount` parameter" (A.6.1.1.5.2.6.1.2.2.1.2.1.2.1.2.1), and `redeemERC4626` likewise "will update the withdrawal rate limit based on the amount of assets received." Reversing an exposure returns the capacity that creating it consumed.

So the mint limit is best read as a **net outstanding exposure meter with a speed governor**, not a spending budget. An Agent that mints and repays promptly retains full capacity; one that mints and holds exhausts it. The cap on the refund at `maxAmount` prevents banking unused headroom, which is what stops an operator from idling to accumulate a burst larger than the bucket was ever meant to permit.

Unlimited is encoded in the same structure — `type(uint256).max` for maxAmount with slope 0 (A.6.1.1.5.2.6.1.2.2.1.3.3) — and short-circuits the arithmetic, so "no limit" is a value in the system rather than an exception to it.
description: getCurrentRateLimit returns min(slope × elapsed + lastAmount, maxAmount), and burnUSDS increases available mint capacity by the amount burned — so the limit tracks net exposure over time.
